issues.legal_issue: The statutory process of arrest and detention for recovering public electricity dues is constitutionally valid.
material_facts: The petitioners owed dues to the State Electricity Board.
The petitioners apprehended that revenue authorities would recover the dues by arrest and detention under the challenged recovery process.
The Supreme Court had, in an earlier decision, upheld the constitutional validity of the same process.
The constitutional validity of the process was the only point pressed in these petitions.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge was rejected and the petitions were dismissed. The revenue authorities could proceed to recover the dues by issuing a fresh process in light of the earlier judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied its earlier decision in Ram Narayan Agarwal v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which upheld the constitutional validity of the process prescribed by Section 279(1)(b), read with Section 281, of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. Recovery of the electricity dues was pursued under the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958, read with Section 279 of the 1950 Act.

predicates.recovery_proceeding_challenges_arrest_pr: The debtors brought a proceeding challenging the constitutionality of arrest and detention as a means of recovering public dues.
predicates.petitioners_owe_recoverable_dues: The persons challenging the recovery process owed dues to a public electricity board.
predicates.same_process_previously_upheld: The Supreme Court had previously considered and upheld the constitutionality of the same arrest-and-detention recovery process.
predicates.challenged_recovery_process_is_constitut: The challenged process of arrest and detention for recovering the dues is constitutionally valid.

issues.definition: When debtors challenge an arrest-and-detention recovery process and the same process has already been upheld, the process is constitutionally valid.
